etymology: From Saxon hyll, a rising of ground. Hebrew gib'ah is a hill or height, from a root meaning to be convex or swelling; it is distinguished in usage from har, a mountain, though the Authorized Version renders both with either word according to sense.
biblical_def: A hill in Scripture is high enough to be seen from below and low enough to be climbed, and both facts are made to preach. Ascent is the question of worship: “Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Psalm 24:3) — and the answer, clean hands and a pure heart, shuts every natural man out until a Mediator brings him. Visibility is the question of witness: “Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Matthew 5:14) — the church's conspicuousness is not a strategy but a condition, and the only choice is whether what is seen is light. The pilgrim lifts his eyes to the hills and then corrects himself as to where help actually lives: “I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help” (Psalm 121:1), which the next verse answers — from the LORD, who made heaven and earth, not from the high places on them. And in the day of the LORD every hill is levelled to make a road for God: “Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low” (Isaiah 40:4). Hills gather worship, false and true; hills expose what is on them; and hills come down when God comes through.
webster_summary: A natural elevation of land, less than a mountain; in Scripture, the hill of the LORD that only clean hands may ascend, the city set on a hill that cannot be hid, the hills to which the pilgrim lifts his eyes, and every hill made low before the coming of God.
webster_full: HILL, n. 1. A natural elevation of land, or a mass of earth rising above the common level of the surrounding land; an eminence less than a mountain.
2. A cluster of earth raised about a plant; as, a hill of maize.
3. In Scripture, the high places on hills were the ordinary sites of idolatrous worship.
4. From Saxon hyll; allied to Latin collis, a hill.
5. In Scripture, who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? Ps. 24; a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid, Matt. 5.
corruption_summary: The visibility of the church is treated as a public-relations problem to be managed rather than a condition God imposed, so that conspicuous holiness is traded for inoffensiveness; and the ascent of God's hill is assumed rather than asked about.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:14 states a fact before it issues a command: a city on a hill cannot be hid. The church has no option of obscurity; her only decision is whether what the world sees is light or the ruins of a lampstand. Much modern strategy proceeds as though the opposite were true — as though the wise course were to lower the profile, soften the distinctives, and become as much like the surrounding plain as possible, on the theory that men will listen to a church they cannot distinguish from themselves. The Lord's own logic runs the other way: let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. A city that succeeds in hiding has not become winsome; it has become salt without savour, and He says plainly what that is good for.

The second failure is at Psalm 24:3, which asks a question the age assumes it has already answered. Who may ascend? The Psalm's reply — he that hath clean hands, and a pure heart — is not a moderate entrance requirement but an absolute bar, since no son of Adam qualifies. Popular religion skips the question entirely and treats access to God as the default condition of being human, needing no atonement and no Mediator. The whole sacrificial system, the veil, the priesthood, and finally the cross exist because the question is real. The one Man with clean hands and a pure heart ascended, and He brings His people up with Him — which is the only answer the Psalm will accept and the only one that leaves the hill holy.
roots_summary: Hebrew gib'ah, a hill or height; har, a mountain or hill country; Greek oros, a mountain, and bounos, a hill or mound.
roots_lines: Hebrew gib'ah (H1389) — a hill or elevation; frequently the site of the high places Israel was commanded to destroy.
Hebrew har (H2022) — a mountain or range of hills; used of Sinai, Zion, and the hill country of Judah.
Hebrew bamah (H1116) — a high place; the standing term for the idolatrous shrines built on hills.
Greek oros (G3735) — a mountain or hill; the mount of the Sermon and the mount of Olives.
Greek bounos (G1015) — a hill or mound; “every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Luke 3:5).
usage: Of the qualification for worship: Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? (Psalm 24:3).
Of the church's unavoidable visibility: A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid (Matthew 5:14).
Of the levelling before God's coming: every mountain and hill shall be made low (Isaiah 40:4).

Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?
Matthew 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Psalm 121:1
A Song of degrees. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.

etymology: From French plain, Latin planus, flat, level, and hence clear or evident — the same word yields both the geography and the moral adjective. Hebrew has several: kikkar, a round district such as the plain of Jordan; 'arabah, the desert rift; and biq'ah, a broad valley between hills.
biblical_def: Level ground is where men gather, and Scripture watches carefully what they build there. Rebellion needed a plain: “as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there” (Genesis 11:2) — and on that flat ground the tower was raised against heaven. Compromise chose a plain too, and by degrees: “Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom” (Genesis 13:12), the well-watered choice made by the eye, and the same plain was later overthrown — “he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities” (Genesis 19:25). Yet the word's other sense turns it into a prayer, because level ground is also safe ground for a man who cannot see far: “Teach me thy way, O LORD, and lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies” (Psalm 27:11). The two senses belong together. The plain is where men build monuments to themselves and where a man may walk without stumbling, and the difference is entirely in who chose the ground. Lot lifted up his eyes and chose; David asked the LORD to lead. Every plain in Scripture is a level place where a heart shows what it wanted.
webster_summary: Level ground, an expanse without hills; also clear, evident, without ornament. In Scripture, the plain of Shinar where Babel was built, the cities of the plain that Lot chose and God overthrew, and the plain path in which the believer asks to be led.
webster_full: PLAIN, a. 1. Smooth; even; level; flat; without elevations or depressions.
2. Open; clear; manifest; evident; not obscure.
3. Artless; simple; without ornament, disguise, or affectation.
4. From Latin planus, level, flat, whence also plane and explain.
5. PLAIN, n. Level ground; an open field. The cities of the plain, Gen. 13; lead me in a plain path, Ps. 27.
corruption_summary: The choice of the well-watered plain is treated as ordinary prudence rather than as the beginning of a ruin, so that decisions made entirely by advantage are never examined; and the plain sense of Scripture is dismissed as naive reading.
corruption_paragraphs: Lot's choice reads as sound business. The plain of Jordan was well watered everywhere, like the garden of the LORD, and he took it; the text records no sin at that moment. What it records is a sequence: he beheld, he chose, he pitched his tent toward Sodom, he dwelt in Sodom, he sat in the gate of Sodom, and he had to be dragged out of Sodom by angels while his wife looked back and his descendants became Moab and Ammon. Scripture's realism about such choices is worth more than a hundred sermons on obvious sins. A decision made purely by visible advantage, with the question of God's glory never raised, does not announce itself as rebellion; it simply sets a direction, and the direction does the rest. Abraham, who let the younger man choose first, received the land by promise.

The word's other sense carries its own controversy, since plain also means evident, and the Reformation staked much on the plain sense of Scripture. That principle is now widely dismissed as naive — the text, it is said, is layered, culturally distant, and available only through expert mediation, so that the ordinary believer with an open Bible is out of his depth. Difficulty in Scripture is real and the Reformers said so; Peter admitted that some things in Paul are hard to be understood. But the perspicuity they confessed was about what is necessary: that the things a man must know for salvation and obedience are set down so plainly that the unlearned may find them. Any doctrine that requires the plain path to be abandoned before a text can be obeyed should be suspected of the same instinct that pitched a tent toward Sodom.
roots_summary: Hebrew kikkar, a round district or plain; 'arabah, the desert plain of the Jordan rift; biq'ah, a broad valley; mishōr, a level place, and so uprightness.
roots_lines: Hebrew kikkar (H3603) — a circuit or round district; the plain of Jordan that Lot chose (Genesis 13:10-12).
Hebrew 'arabah (H6160) — the desert plain, especially the rift running from Galilee to the Red Sea.
Hebrew biq'ah (H1237) — a broad valley or plain between mountains; the plain of Shinar (Genesis 11:2).
Hebrew mishōr (H4334) — a level place, and figuratively equity or uprightness; the plain path of Psalm 27:11.
Greek pedinos (G3977) — level, flat; “stood in the plain” (Luke 6:17).
usage: Of the ground of Babel's pride: they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there (Genesis 11:2).
Of a choice made by the eye: Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:12).
Of the path the believer asks for: lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies (Psalm 27:11).

Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom.
Genesis 19:25
And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.

Teach me thy way, O LORD, and lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies.

etymology: A compound of high and way — a road raised above the surrounding ground, and so a public road maintained for common passage. Hebrew mesillah is from salal, to cast up or raise a bank, and means precisely that: a causeway built up by labour, not a track worn by feet.
biblical_def: A highway in Scripture is a made road — something raised, cleared, and kept — and it is one of the Bible's great gospel figures. Isaiah announces that God will have such a road built for His own coming: “Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God” (Isaiah 40:3), the verse John the Baptist took as the description of his ministry. Isaiah then names the road itself and fences it: “an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it” (Isaiah 35:8) — a public road, open and plain, and yet closed to the unclean, which is the gospel's exact combination of freeness and holiness. Proverbs gives the same road a moral surface: “The highway of the upright is to depart from evil: he that keepeth his way preserveth his soul” (Proverbs 16:17). And the Lord Jesus sends the invitation out to the roads themselves when the invited will not come: “Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled” (Luke 14:23). The figure is consistent. God builds the road, the road is holy, the road is public, and the servants are sent to the roadside to bring in the people no one expected.
webster_summary: A public road raised above the common level; a main road open to all. In Scripture, the highway made straight in the desert for God, the highway called The way of holiness which the unclean shall not pass over, the highway of the upright, and the highways into which servants are sent to compel men in.
webster_full: HIGHWAY, n. 1. A public road; a way open to all passengers; so called either because it is a great or public road, or because it is raised above the adjacent ground.
2. Course; road; figuratively, a way of life or conduct.
3. In Scripture, a raised causeway prepared for the passage of a king.
4. From high and way; Hebrew mesillah, from salal, to cast up a bank.
5. In Scripture, make straight in the desert a highway for our God, Isa. 40; go out into the highways and hedges, Luke 14.
corruption_summary: The way of holiness is widened until no one is excluded and the road ceases to lead anywhere in particular; or, at the other extreme, “compel them to come in” is made a warrant for coercion in religion.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 35:8 holds two things together that the age insists on separating. The road is a highway — public, plain, so clear that wayfaring men though fools shall not err therein — and it is fenced: the unclean shall not pass over it. Modern religion keeps the first clause and deletes the second, so that the way becomes a broad avenue on which every traveller is already walking and the notion of exclusion is thought cruel. Our Lord's own words are the answer: strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it. The gospel is genuinely free — whosoever will may come — but the road it opens is the way of holiness, and a religion that promises the destination while denying the road is not generous; it is a false direction given to travellers who will not discover the error until too late.

The opposite corruption took Luke 14:23 and made a weapon of it. Augustine's appeal to compelle intrare against the Donatists was used for centuries to justify the civil sword in matters of religion, and the medieval and even some Protestant establishments pressed men into conformity by law. The parable will not bear it. The servant is sent out with an invitation to a supper, and the compelling is the earnest urgency of a messenger pressing men who cannot believe they are wanted — the poor, the maimed, the halt, the blind, gathered from the roadside. The 1689 Confession states the principle recovered at great cost: God alone is Lord of the conscience, and faith is not produced by force. The urgency belongs in the preaching; the magistrate's sword has no business on this highway.
roots_summary: Hebrew mesillah, a raised causeway or highway, from salal, to cast up; ma'gal, a track or path; Greek hodos, a way, and diexodos, an outlet or crossroad.
roots_lines: Hebrew mesillah (H4546) — a raised highway or causeway; the road prepared for the LORD's coming (Isaiah 40:3).
Hebrew salal (H5549) — to cast up, to raise a bank or road; “cast up the highway” (Isaiah 62:10).
Hebrew derek (H1870) — a way, road, or manner of life; the ordinary word joined to mesillah in Isaiah 35:8.
Greek hodos (G3598) — a way or road; the name by which Christianity was first known, “this way” (Acts 9:2).
Greek diexodos (G1327) — a way out, a place where roads part; “the highways” of Matthew 22:9.
usage: Of the road prepared for God's coming: make straight in the desert a highway for our God (Isaiah 40:3).
Of the fenced public way: it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it (Isaiah 35:8).
Of the gospel invitation carried outward: Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in (Luke 14:23).

The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.
Isaiah 35:8

And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.
Proverbs 16:17
The highway of the upright is to depart from evil: he that keepeth his way preserveth his soul.
Luke 14:23
And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.

etymology: From Latin cavus, hollow, through French cave. The limestone of Judea is riddled with them, and Scripture uses caves for exactly what the land afforded them for — burial, refuge, and hiding — so that the same hollow may be a tomb, a fortress, or a place of shame.
biblical_def: The cave is where Scripture buries its dead, hides its fugitives, and meets its discouraged prophets. Abraham's first legal foothold in the promised land is a grave bought at full price: “That he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he hath, which is in the end of his field” (Genesis 23:9) — a patriarch who owned nothing of Canaan but a tomb, and held it as a pledge of a promise he died believing. The cave is refuge for the anointed and rejected: “David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam” (1 Samuel 22:1), where the distressed, the indebted, and the discontented gathered to him — a king's first court held in a hole in the ground. It is also where a great man hides after a great victory: “he came thither unto a cave, and lodged there; and, behold, the word of the LORD came to him” (1 Kings 19:9), and the question that follows — What doest thou here, Elijah? — is God's way of fetching a servant out of self-pity. The epistle to the Hebrews gathers the whole class of such men in one clause: “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Hebrews 11:38), with the verdict attached, of whom the world was not worthy. And the grave of Lazarus was one: “It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it” (John 11:38) — until a voice called into it.
webster_summary: A hollow place in the earth; a den or cavern. In Scripture, the cave of Machpelah bought for a burying place, the cave of Adullam where David gathered his men, the cave in which Elijah lodged and was questioned by God, and the caves in which the persecuted faithful wandered.
webster_full: CAVE, n. 1. A hollow place in the earth; a subterraneous cavern; a den.
2. A hollow; any hollow place, as in a rock or under a bank.
3. A place of retreat or concealment; hence, a refuge.
4. From Latin cavus, hollow; French cave.
5. In Scripture, the cave of Machpelah, Gen. 23; escaped to the cave Adullam, 1 Sam. 22.
corruption_summary: Withdrawal is romanticised as spirituality, so that the cave becomes a destination rather than a shelter; and the faithful who actually lived in them are read as failures rather than as men of whom the world was not worthy.
corruption_paragraphs: Elijah's cave is the Bible's own correction of the instinct to retreat. He had won at Carmel and fled from a woman's threat, and God's dealing with him is a model of pastoral wisdom: sleep, food, a second meal, and only then a question — What doest thou here, Elijah? The Lord does not commend the cave, does not scold the exhaustion, and does not leave him there. He gives him the still small voice, corrects his belief that he alone was left by naming seven thousand, and then sends him back to work with three commissions. The monastic instinct, ancient and modern, gets this backwards, treating withdrawal as the higher path and mistaking solitude for sanctity. Scripture allows retreat — our Lord Himself went apart to pray — but always as a place to be refuelled and never as a place to live.

The other misreading is worldlier. Hebrews 11 lists men who were tortured, stoned, sawn asunder, and who wandered in dens and caves of the earth, and the prosperity teaching of our day has no category for them at all. On its accounting, a believer in a cave is a believer whose faith failed to produce, since faith is supposed to yield health, standing, and increase. The Spirit's verdict on those cave-dwellers is the exact reverse: of whom the world was not worthy. The principle to recover is that visible outcome is no index of divine favour. Abraham owned one cave in the land of promise and was not disappointed; David reigned from a cave before he reigned from a throne; and the roll of faith ends with men who received not the promise in this life because God had provided some better thing.
roots_summary: Hebrew me'arah, a cave or cavern; mechillah, a hole or burrow; Greek spēlaion, a cave or den.

Hebrew mechillah (H4247) — a hole or burrow; the caves of the rocks men flee into at the terror of the LORD (Isaiah 2:19).
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — a rock or cliff; the clefts of the rock in which Moses was hidden (Exodus 33:22).
Greek spēlaion (G4693) — a cave or den; the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:38) and the den of thieves (Matthew 21:13).
Greek opē (G3692) — a hole or opening; “in dens and caves of the earth” (Hebrews 11:38).
usage: Of the patriarch's only holding in the land: the cave of Machpelah... for as much money as it is worth (Genesis 23:9).
Of refuge for the anointed and rejected: escaped to the cave Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1).
Of the faithful driven underground: they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth (Hebrews 11:38).

That he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he hath, which is in the end of his field; for as much money as it is worth he shall give it me for a possession of a buryingplace amongst you. as

David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam: and when his brethren and all his father's house heard it, they went down thither to him.
1 Kings 19:9
And he came thither unto a cave, and lodged there; and, behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said unto him, What doest thou here, Elijah?

etymology: From Saxon denn, a cave or lair of a beast. The word keeps its animal sense throughout Scripture: a den is where a predator lives and where it drags what it has taken, which is why the Lord's use of it for the temple courts is so severe.
biblical_def: A den is a lair, and Scripture uses it for the places where dangerous things are at home. Daniel's trial is the plainest: “Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions” (Daniel 6:16) — a man condemned by a law framed against his prayers, delivered not from the den but in it. Jeremiah takes the same word for what the temple had become in the hands of men who sinned all week and sheltered in it on the sabbath: “Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?” (Jeremiah 7:11). Our Lord quotes that verse when He overturns the tables: “My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Matthew 21:13). The charge is precise and worth hearing exactly. A den is not where thieves rob; it is where they retire after robbing, feeling safe. The accusation is not merely that the temple traffic was dishonest but that religion had become the hiding place of men who intended to keep their sin. And the last use is a promise that the lair itself will be harmless: “the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den” (Isaiah 11:8) — a world under Messiah's reign where a child may reach into the place of death and take no hurt.
webster_summary: A cave or hollow place; the lair of a wild beast. In Scripture, the den of lions into which Daniel was cast, the temple made a den of robbers and of thieves, and the cockatrice' den on which a weaned child shall safely put his hand.
webster_full: DEN, n. 1. A cave or hollow place in the earth; usually the retreat of a wild beast.
2. Any squalid or wretched place of resort.
3. A place of retreat and security for men of evil design; as, a den of thieves.
4. From Saxon denn, a cave, a lair.
5. In Scripture, cast him into the den of lions, Dan. 6; ye have made it a den of thieves, Matt. 21.
corruption_summary: The cleansing of the temple is reduced to a protest against commerce or unjust pricing, missing the charge Christ actually made — that the house of prayer had become the refuge of unrepentant men.
corruption_paragraphs: The temple cleansing is now most often preached as an economic protest: the money changers overcharged, the poor were exploited, and Christ acted for the marginalised. Exploitation there certainly was, and Scripture never excuses it. But the verse He quoted supplies the actual indictment, and Jeremiah 7 leaves no ambiguity about it. The prophet lists the sins — stealing, murder, adultery, false swearing, burning incense unto Baal — and then says the people came and stood before God in His house and said, We are delivered to do all these abominations. That is a den: a place where predators feel safe. The Lord's charge against the temple traffic is that religion had been converted into cover, and the cover is what enraged Him. Any church that offers men assurance without repentance is running the same establishment with better music.

Daniel's den corrects a different modern instinct, which reads deliverance as escape from trouble. Daniel was not spared the den; he was put into it, and God shut the lions' mouths while he was inside. The distinction matters pastorally, because most believers are not delivered from their trials but kept through them. The king's decree had been framed precisely to catch a man who prayed, and Daniel went home and prayed with his windows open toward Jerusalem as he did aforetime — the whole strength of the account lying in that phrase, as he did aforetime. He did not increase his devotion to meet the crisis or reduce it to survive; he continued. The principle to recover is that faithfulness before the test is what carries a man through it.
roots_summary: Hebrew me'ōnah, a lair or dwelling of beasts; Aramaic gob, a pit or den; Greek spēlaion, a cave used as a lair.
roots_lines: Hebrew me'ōnah (H4585) — a den or habitation, especially of lions; “the lion's den” (Nahum 2:12).
Aramaic gob (H1358) — a pit or den; the word used throughout Daniel 6 for the lions' den.
Hebrew me'arah (H4631) — a cave; the word Jeremiah uses for the den of robbers (Jeremiah 7:11).
Greek spēlaion (G4693) — a cave or den; “a den of thieves” (Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Luke 19:46).
Greek lēstēs (G3027) — a robber or brigand, not a petty thief; the violent word behind “den of thieves.”
usage: Of preservation in the trial rather than from it: cast him into the den of lions (Daniel 6:16).
Of religion turned into cover for sin: Is this house... become a den of robbers in your eyes? (Jeremiah 7:11).
Of the peace of Messiah's reign: the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den (Isaiah 11:8).

Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spake and said unto Daniel, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee.

Matthew 21:13

etymology: From Saxon dic, a trench or dike — the same word gives both ditch, the hollow dug, and dike, the bank thrown up beside it. In Scripture the ditch is usually a pit: something a man digs, and something a man falls into, and the two are often the same man.
biblical_def: The ditch in Scripture is a trap, and it is remarkable how often the digger is the victim. David states it as a settled providence: “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made” (Psalm 7:15) — not an accident but a moral order, in which mischief returns upon the head that devised it. Job uses the word for the utter defilement of a man before a holy God, and the honesty of it is bracing: even if he washed himself with snow water, “yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me” (Job 9:31) — self-cleansing cannot survive contact with God's holiness. The Lord Jesus makes the ditch the destination of a whole method of religion: “they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch” (Matthew 15:14) — teacher and taught in the same hole, which is the most sobering thing ever said about false teaching. And once, memorably, God commands ditches be dug as an act of faith before there is any sign of water: “Thus saith the LORD, Make this valley full of ditches” (2 Kings 3:16), and the water came without wind or rain. The ditch a man digs for his brother takes him; the ditch a man digs at God's word is filled.
webster_summary: A trench in the earth made by digging; a pit or hollow. In Scripture, the ditch a man digs and falls into himself, the ditch of defilement in Job, the ditch into which the blind leading the blind must fall, and the ditches dug at the LORD's command and filled without rain.
webster_full: DITCH, n. 1. A trench in the earth made by digging, particularly a trench for draining wet land, or for making a fence.
2. Any long hollow receptacle of water.
3. A pit or hole into which one may fall.
4. From Saxon dic, a ditch or dike; the same word as dike, the bank thrown up from the trench.
5. In Scripture, is fallen into the ditch which he made, Ps. 7; both shall fall into the ditch, Matt. 15.
corruption_summary: False teaching is treated as a private mistake affecting only the teacher, when Scripture says the blind guide takes his hearers into the pit with him; and the digging of ditches by God's word is replaced by strategies that require no faith at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 15:14 is the reason the New Testament is so severe about teachers. Error is not contained in the man who holds it; it travels down every rank that trusts him, and the Lord's picture has the guide and the guided ending in the same ditch. James warns that teachers receive the greater condemnation; Paul tells Timothy to take heed unto himself and unto the doctrine, for in so doing he shall both save himself and them that hear him. The modern reluctance to name false teachers — on the grounds that it is unkind, divisive, or above our pay grade — is measured against a Lord who called the leading religious authorities of His day blind guides to their faces, and told His disciples plainly to let them alone. Charity toward persons is not owed to their doctrine.

The second use of the ditch is a rebuke to a different kind of blindness. Elisha told three kings to dig ditches in a dry valley with no cloud in the sky, and the digging was the whole of their part; God supplied the water. Faith of that shape is rare because it looks foolish until it is vindicated, and church planning increasingly prefers methods that will work whether or not God moves. There is no virtue in digging ditches nobody was told to dig, and Scripture nowhere commends recklessness. But where God has given a word — preach, pray, gather, disciple, endure — obedience is to dig, in dry ground, before the water comes. The valley filled without wind and without rain, and every man who had refused to dig had a trench-shaped share of nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachath, a pit or corruption; gēb, a cistern or trench; Greek bothunos, a pit or hole in the ground.

etymology: From Saxon banc, a ridge or bench — the same root gives the bench a moneychanger sat at, whence the modern financial sense. Scripture uses all three: the raised edge of a river, the siege mound cast up against a city, and the table at which money was put out to increase.
biblical_def: The English word gathers three distinct things in Scripture, and each carries weight. It is the edge of a river, where God's power over the waters is displayed: Pharaoh dreams that “I stood upon the bank of the river” (Genesis 41:17), and Israel comes to a Jordan in flood — “Jordan overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest” (Joshua 3:15) — at precisely the season when crossing was impossible, which is why the crossing proved who had brought them. It is the siege mound thrown up against a city: “they cast up a bank against the city, and it stood in the trench” (2 Samuel 20:15) — the patient earthwork of a besieger who intends to take what is behind the wall. And it is the moneychanger's table in the Lord's parable of the pounds, where the unprofitable servant is condemned out of his own excuse: “Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank, that at my coming I might have required mine own with usury?” (Luke 19:23). That third use is the sharpest. The servant who did nothing thought caution was safety, and the Lord answers that even the least venture — putting the sum where it would at least gain interest — would have been better than burying it. Stewardship admits of no neutral option; what is not employed for the Master is withheld from Him.
webster_summary: A ridge of earth; the margin of a river; a mound cast up in a siege; and a bench or table for money, whence an establishment for its keeping. In Scripture, the bank of the river in Pharaoh's dream, Jordan overflowing its banks, the bank cast up against a city, and the bank the slothful servant would not use.
webster_full: BANK, n. 1. A ridge of earth raised above the surrounding plain; a mound.
2. The margin or border of a river, lake, or sea.
3. A bench or table; hence, a place where money is deposited and put to use.
4. From Saxon banc, a bench or ridge; the money sense from the bench of the exchanger.
5. In Scripture, Jordan overfloweth all his banks, Josh. 3; gavest not thou my money into the bank, Luke 19.
corruption_summary: Doing nothing is mistaken for doing no harm, so that the servant who buries what he was given supposes himself safe; and the parable's mention of interest is pressed into a general endorsement or condemnation of lending at usury.
corruption_paragraphs: The unprofitable servant is the most reassuring figure in the parable to a certain kind of churchgoer, and the most alarming once the Lord answers him. He did nothing wrong in the ordinary sense: he stole nothing, spent nothing, lost nothing, and returned exactly what he had received. His condemnation is that he treated caution as fidelity. The Master's reply cuts off the excuse at its root — if you really believed I was an austere man reaping where I sowed not, that belief should have produced action, not paralysis. Sloth is here exposed as a form of unbelief that flatters itself as prudence. Every gift, office, and opportunity given to a Christian falls under the same accounting, and the question at the reckoning will not be whether he avoided error but what he did with what he was handed.

The mention of interest requires care, since Scripture forbids usury toward a poor brother in Israel (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36-37) while the parable assumes commercial lending without censure. The distinction the law draws is between exploiting a brother's distress and ordinary commercial exchange, and the prophets denounce the first, not the second. The parable is not a treatise on finance; it takes an ordinary commercial fact as the minimum the servant might have done. The principle to recover is the parable's own: the Master gives according to His will, expects increase according to His gift, and reckons with every servant personally. Faithfulness is measured against what was entrusted, which is why the man with two pounds and the man with ten receive the same commendation, and the man who buried one receives none.
roots_summary: Hebrew saphah, a lip, edge, or bank; gadah, a river bank; sol'lah, a siege mound cast up; Greek trapeza, a table, and thence a bank.

etymology: From Saxon wind, cognate with Latin ventus. In both biblical tongues the word for wind is also the word for breath and for spirit — Hebrew ruach, Greek pneuma — so that the natural fact and the supernatural Person are named together, and Scripture repeatedly moves between the two in a single sentence.
biblical_def: Wind is the standing figure for what is real, powerful, and beyond human management. The Lord Jesus uses it to explain the new birth to a ruler who wanted a mechanism: “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8) — the effects are unmistakable and the cause is sovereign and unseen. At Pentecost the figure becomes a sign: “suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2). The same word describes emptiness and judgment: “they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hosea 8:7) — sin returns with interest and in kind. And James uses it for the unstable soul: the doubter “is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (James 1:6). Taken together the uses set an antithesis. There is a wind that blows where it will and gives life, and there is a wind a man sows and is destroyed by; there is a Spirit who fills a house, and there is a gust that drives a man who will not be anchored. What no use of the figure ever allows is that the wind might be produced, steered, or scheduled by the men it moves.
webster_summary: Air in motion; a current of air; by figure, breath, spirit, and also that which is empty or unstable. In Scripture, the wind that bloweth where it listeth as an image of the new birth, the rushing mighty wind of Pentecost, sowing the wind and reaping the whirlwind, and the doubter driven with the wind and tossed.
webster_full: WIND, n. 1. Air in motion with any degree of velocity, from the gentlest breeze to the most violent storm.
2. Breath; power of respiration.
3. Anything insignificant or light as wind; empty words; vanity.
4. From Saxon wind; Latin ventus. Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma denote wind, breath, and spirit alike.
5. In Scripture, the wind bloweth where it listeth, John 3; they have sown the wind, Hos. 8.
corruption_summary: The Spirit's sovereign freedom is either domesticated into a technique that can produce revival on demand, or spiritualised into a vague and undoctrinal atmosphere that no longer requires the new birth at all.
corruption_paragraphs: John 3:8 was spoken to a man who wanted a method, and the answer withholds one. The wind blows where it listeth; Nicodemus cannot arrange it, and neither can the church. The revivalist tradition after Finney reversed this deliberately, teaching that a revival is not a miracle but the right use of the appointed means — which in practice meant techniques for producing decisions, and produced a century of manufactured awakenings with little fruit. The charismatic wing repeats the error with different machinery, working the room until something happens and calling the result the Spirit. Both make the wind a thing men raise. Scripture leaves the church with means she is commanded to use — preaching, prayer, the ordinances, holy living — and leaves the wind with God, which is exactly why revival is asked for and never engineered.

The opposite corruption empties the figure. Where spirit becomes a vague word for atmosphere, uplift, or the better part of human nature, the new birth ceases to be a supernatural act and becomes a change of outlook, and men are told they need encouragement rather than resurrection. The Lord's words to Nicodemus close that door: except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God, and the birth is of the Spirit, not of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man. The principle to recover holds both truths without compromise. The Spirit is sovereign and unmanageable, so no man may claim to produce Him; and He is really and powerfully at work, so no man may reduce Him to a mood.
roots_summary: Hebrew ruach, wind, breath, or spirit; se'arah, a whirlwind or tempest; Greek anemos, wind, and pneuma, wind, breath, or the Holy Ghost.

Greek pnoē (G4157) — a blowing or breath; “a rushing mighty wind” at Pentecost (Acts 2:2).

etymology: From Latin palatium, the Palatine hill in Rome where the emperors built, whence every royal house in Europe took its name. Hebrew armon is a fortified citadel or great house; bīrah, a castle or palace, used of Shushan and of the temple itself as the palace of the LORD.
biblical_def: A palace is a king's house, and Scripture measures every one of them against the house of the great King. David corrects the whole ambition of temple-building with a single clause: “the palace is not for man, but for the LORD God” (1 Chronicles 29:1) — the most magnificent building Israel ever raised was not a monument to Solomon, and David says so while handing over the plans. The bride of Psalm 45 is brought into a royal house with joy: “With gladness and rejoicing shall they be brought: they shall enter into the king's palace” (Psalm 45:15), a marriage psalm the New Testament applies to Christ and His church. But a palace is also where power conspires: “Then assembled together the chief priests, and the scribes, and the elders of the people, unto the palace of the high priest” (Matthew 26:3) — the plot against the Lord of glory was laid in a fine house by respectable men. And the gospel walks into a palace on its own terms in Paul's report from prison: “my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace, and in all other places” (Philippians 1:13) — a chained prisoner evangelising Caesar's household guard by rotation. The pattern is consistent: palaces impress, palaces conspire, palaces fall; and the gospel enters them not as a suppliant but as a prisoner who is free.
webster_summary: The house in which a king or great personage dwells; a splendid dwelling. In Scripture, the temple as a palace not for man but for the LORD God, the king's palace into which the bride is brought, the high priest's palace where Christ's death was plotted, and Caesar's palace where Paul's bonds preached Christ.
webster_full: PALACE, n. 1. A magnificent house in which an emperor, king, or other distinguished person resides.
2. A splendid place of residence; hence, any large and stately building.
3. In Scripture, a citadel or fortified house; the temple is called the palace of the LORD.
4. From Latin palatium, from the Palatine hill in Rome, the site of the imperial residence.
5. In Scripture, the palace is not for man, but for the LORD God, 1 Chron. 29; manifest in all the palace, Phil. 1.
corruption_summary: Magnificence in religious building is defended as glory given to God when it is often glory taken for men; and the church, seeking influence, courts the palace rather than preaching to it.
corruption_paragraphs: David's sentence about the temple — the palace is not for man, but for the LORD God — is the standard against which every grand religious building must be measured, and it cuts in an uncomfortable direction. The question is not whether beauty in worship is permissible; Scripture lavishes gold and blue and scarlet on the tabernacle at God's own command, and the regulative principle governs the elements of worship, not the plainness of the room. The question is whose name the building carries in practice. Cathedrals raised on indulgence money, and the modern auditorium built to a personality, fail the same test from opposite directions. A church may build well and to the glory of God; it may not build to be seen, and the difference is usually visible to everyone except the builders.

The second temptation is proximity to power. The chief priests met in a palace to plot the death of Christ, and the church has repeatedly wanted a seat in that room ever since — sometimes for protection, sometimes for influence, sometimes for the plain pleasure of being consulted. Paul entered the palace by a different door. He was in chains, in Caesar's custody, and the result was that his bonds in Christ were manifest in all the palace, with saints of Caesar's household sending greetings by the end of the letter. The principle to recover is that the church addresses palaces prophetically, not politically: she owes the magistrate honour and obedience in his sphere, she owes him the truth about the Lord who will judge him, and she owes him no flattery at all.

etymology: From French prison, Latin prensio, a seizing, from prehendo, to take hold of — the place of those who have been taken. Greek phylakē is literally a guarding or watch, the same word used for the watches of the night, so that a prison is named for the guard rather than for the walls.
biblical_def: Scripture is full of prisons, and remarkably free of the assumption that they are proof of guilt. Joseph, Jeremiah, Micaiah, John the Baptist, Peter, and Paul were all in them, and God's people are commanded to remember such: “I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Matthew 25:36), where the Lord identifies Himself so closely with His imprisoned people that visiting them is visiting Him. The messianic commission promises release: the Servant is sent “to open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house” (Isaiah 42:7), a liberty first spiritual and finally complete. At Philippi God shows what a prison is worth against Him: “suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken” (Acts 16:26) — and the astonishing detail is that the prisoners did not run, so that the gaoler was converted before dawn. And Peter records a preaching in a place no man could visit: Christ “went and preached unto the spirits in prison” (1 Peter 3:19). Whatever the difficulty of that verse, its plain force is that no confinement is beyond His reach or His voice. The doctrine of prison in Scripture is therefore twofold: the state may lawfully hold men, and it repeatedly holds the wrong ones; and God is not shut out of any cell.
webster_summary: A place of confinement for those seized or condemned; a gaol. In Scripture, the prison in which the righteous are so often found, Christ counting a visit to the imprisoned as done to Himself, the Servant sent to bring prisoners out of the prison house, and the prison at Philippi shaken to its foundations.
webster_full: PRISON, n. 1. A house or place of confinement, particularly for debtors and criminals; a gaol.
2. Any place of confinement or involuntary restraint.
3. Figuratively, a state of bondage from which one cannot free himself.
4. From French prison, Latin prehensio, a seizing, from prehendo, to seize.
5. In Scripture, I was in prison, and ye came unto me, Matt. 25; the foundations of the prison were shaken, Acts 16.
corruption_summary: Imprisonment is read as a reliable index of guilt, so that the church forgets a duty Christ commanded; while in the other direction, the state's lawful power of the sword is denied altogether and justice reduced to therapy.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 25:36 places visiting the imprisoned among the acts by which Christ identifies His own, and the church has often found it the easiest of them to neglect. Part of the reason is a quiet assumption that a man in prison has earned his place there, and therefore that ministry to him is optional charity rather than commanded duty. Scripture's own roll of prisoners — Joseph on a false accusation, Jeremiah in the dungeon of Malchiah, John the Baptist for naming a king's adultery, Paul in chains for the hope of Israel — forbids the assumption. The Lord does not distinguish, in that passage, between the justly and unjustly held; He commands the visit. And the gospel has always found prisons unusually fruitful ground, because a man there has fewer illusions left about his own condition.

The opposite error denies the magistrate's sword. Romans 13 gives the civil ruler a real ministry of justice, bearing the sword to execute wrath upon evildoers, and Scripture nowhere treats punishment as a failure of compassion. Where the state is stripped of that office and crime is reclassified wholly as illness, the wronged are left without redress and the wrongdoer without the moral seriousness of being held responsible — which is itself a denial of his dignity as a man made in God's image and answerable for his acts. The principle to recover holds both: justice is God's ordinance and must be done, and mercy to the imprisoned is God's command and must be shown. Paul sang at midnight in a gaol he had done nothing to deserve, and the gaoler who had locked him in was washing his stripes before morning.
roots_summary: Hebrew beth ha-sōhar, the round house or prison of Joseph; masgēr, a lock-up or dungeon; Greek phylakē, a guard or ward, and desmōtērion, a place of bonds.
